question: Explain the internal architecture of 8085 microprocessor with labeled block diagram.
answer:
The 8085 microprocessor is 8-bit general purpose microprocessor capable of addressing 16K of memory. The device has 40 pins which required +5V single phase power supply and can operate with 3MHz single phase clock.

The 8085 is an enhanced/ improved version of its previous model 8080. Its instruction is upward compatible with that of 8080. It was most popular microprocessor for commercial purpose of 8 bit.

This microprocessor contain 3 buses i.e Address, Data and Control. Address bus is of 16 bit i.e 216 = 64 kb of data can be recognized by at a single cycle in single operation by address bus. Data bus carries data required from recognized bus and control bus will help for the read/ write operation. The size of data bus is 8-bit, therefore 8085 microprocessor is also called 8-bit microprocessor. All the signals in 8085 microprocessor can be classified into six groups and they are:

  • Address bus
  • Data bus
  • Control and status signal
  • Power supply and frequency signal
  • Externally initiated signal
  • Serial I/O ports

The block diagram of 8085 is as follow:

Components of 8085 Microprocessor:

  • Accumulator (A): It is an 8-bit register that stores the outcomes of operations and is a component of the Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU).
  • Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU): carries out logical (AND, OR, NOT) and arithmetic (addition, subtraction) operations.
  • General Purpose Registers (B, C, D, E, H, L): There are six 8-bit registers (BC, DE, HL) that can be utilized separately or in pairs of 16 bits.
  • Program Counter (PC): The memory address of the subsequent instruction to be executed is stored in a 16-bit register called the Program Counter (PC).
  • Stack Pointer (SP): a 16-bit register that indicates the memory stack’s top.
  • Instruction Register (IR): retains the active instruction while it is being decoded and carried out.
  • Instruction Decoder: produces control signals after decoding the instruction that was retrieved from memory.
  • Control Unit (CU): coordinates with other elements to oversee the way instructions are carried out.
  • Address Bus: Memory addresses are sent from the CPU to memory or I/O devices via a 16-bit unidirectional bus.
  • Data Bus: Data is transferred between the CPU, memory, and I/O devices via an 8-bit bidirectional bus.
  • Timing and Control Unit: produces timing signals to ensure that processes are properly synchronized.
  • Interrupt Control: Prioritizes work by managing internal and external interruptions.
  • Serial I/O Control: used with SID (Serial Input Data) and SOD (Serial Output Data) pins for serial communication.

question: Write short notes in (any two):  Flags in 8085 MPU DMA
answer:
a. Flags in 8085 MPU:
ALU includes five flip-flops (flags), which are set or reset after an operation according to the data conditions of the result in the accumulator and other registers, indicating the status of different states separately. These flags are:
S – Sign Flag
After the execution of an arithmetic/logic operation, if D7 bit (MSB) of result is 1, sign flag (S) is set. D7 bit indicates the sign.
Z – Zero Flag
 Set if the result of the last operation is 0. Used in loop control and in searching a particular data value.
AC – Auxiliary Carry Flag
In an arithmetic operation, when a carry is generated by D3 bit and passed to D4 bit, AC flag is set. Only internally used for BCD operations and not available for the programmer.
P – Parity Flag
Set if the number of 1s in the result of the last operation is even.
CY – Carry Flag
 Set if the result of the last operation generates carry.

b. DMA:
Direct Memory Access (DMA) is a module where a seperate hardware is used which is responsible for transfer of data from i/o without involvement of the CPU. It is a technique that allows peripherals to transfer data directly to or from the main memory without involving the CPU in data handling.

Working of DMA is explained below as:
The peripherals request the DMA controller for the transfer of the data from memory or to memory.
DMA request for the bus from CPU. When CPU gets the bus request from the DMA then the CPU acknowledges the DMA in response to the request and grant the bus to the DMA.
When the DMA gets the access of the bus then the DMA sends the acknowledgment to the I/O.
When the acknowledge is received then the I/O and memory uses the granted bus and perform data transfer using it.
Once the data transmission is completed then the I/O returns the bus to the CPU goes back to the normal working.

question: Explain Register Organization in 80386 microprocessor.
answer:
The register organization of 80386 is given below as:

  • The 80386 microprocessor has eight 32 – bit general purposr registers which may be used as either 8 bit or 16 bit register.
  • A 32 bit register known as an extended register is represented by the register name with prefix E. example : A 32 bit register correspondingto AX is EAX, similarly BX is EBX etc.
  • The 16 bit registers BP, SP, SI and DI in 8086 are now available with thwir extended size of 32 bit and are named as EBP, ESP, ESI and EDI.
  • AX represents the lower 16 bit of the 32 bit register EAX.
  • BP, SP, SI and DI represents the lower 16 bit of their 32 bit counterparts and can be used as independent 16 bit registers.
  • The six segment register available in 80386 are CS, SS, DS, ES, FS and GS.
  • The CS and SS are the code and the stack segment registers respectively , while DS, ES, FS, GS are 4 data segment registers.
  • A 16 bit instruction pointer IP is available along with 32 bit counterpart EIP.

question: Explain different addressing modes in 8085 mocroprocessor.
answer:
The method by which the address of the source of data or the address of the destination of the result is given in the instruction.

Types:

  1. Direct Addressing Mode
  2. Register Direct Addressing Mode
  3. Register Indirect Addressing Mode
  4. Immediate Addressing Mode
  5. Implied Addressing Mode

 

  1. Direct Addressing Mode: Instructions specify the effective address as part of the instruction. Here, the address of the operand is given in the instruction itself.
    Example:
    LDA 2500H: Loads the content of memory location 2500H into the accumulator.
    Explanation:
    LDA is the operation.
    2500H is the address of the source.
    Accumulator is the destination.
  2. Register Direct Addressing Mode: Here, the operand is in a general-purpose register. The data is provided through registers.
    Example:
    MOV A, B: Moves the contents of register B to A.
    Explanation:
    MOV is the operation.
    B is the source of data.
    A is the destination.
  3. Register Indirect Addressing Mode: Here, the address part of the instruction specifies the memory location whose content is the address of the operand. In 8085, whenever instructions use the HL pointer, the address is called indirect addressing.
    Example:
    MOV A, M: Moves data from a memory location (specified by the HL register pair) to the accumulator.
    Explanation:
    MOV is the operation.
    M is the source (memory location specified by HL pair).
    A is the destination.
  4. Immediate Addressing Mode: Here, the operand is specified within the instruction itself.
    Examples:
    MVI A, 05H: Moves 05H into the accumulator.
    LXI H, 7A21H: Loads register H with 7A and register L with 21.
  5. Implied Addressing Mode: The address is implied by the instruction, and no specific operand is mentioned in the instruction itself.

question: Explain about memory segment and segment register in 8086 microprocessor.
answer:
The 8086 microprocessor’s Segment Unit uses 16-bit segment registers and a 16-bit offset to create the 20-bit physical address. Up to 1 MB of memory may be accessed by the 8086 thanks to it. This is how it operates:There are 4 16-bit segment registers, namely: CS, SS, DS, ES.

  1. CS :
    It stands for Code Segment. Used for addressing 64 KB memory location in the code segment of memory where the code of the executable program is stored.
  2. DS :
    It stands for Data Segment. Points to the data segment of 64 KB memory where data is stored.
  3. ES:
    It stands for Extra Segment. Refers to another data segment of the memory.
  4. SS:
    It stands for Stack Segment. Used for addressing the stack segment of memory.

question: Write an ALP to convert the string "computer science" to upper case using 16 bit microprocessor.
answer:
DATA SEGMENT
    STR DB 'computer science$', 0  ; Input string with '$' as terminator
    RESULT DB 20 DUP('$')          ; Space to store the result
DATA ENDS

CODE SEGMENT
    ASSUME CS:CODE, DS:DATA
START:
    MOV AX, DATA                   ; Load the data segment
    MOV DS, AX

    LEA SI, STR                    ; Load address of input string into SI
    LEA DI, RESULT                 ; Load address of result buffer into DI

NEXT_CHAR:
    LODSB                          ; Load the next character from STR to AL
    CMP AL, '$'                    ; Check for string terminator
    JE END_CONVERT                 ; If found, end conversion

    CMP AL, 'a'                    ; Check if character is lower case
    JL COPY_CHAR                   ; If less, it is not a lower-case letter
    CMP AL, 'z'
    JG COPY_CHAR                   ; If greater, it is not a lower-case letter

    SUB AL, 20H                    ; Convert to upper case by subtracting 0x20

COPY_CHAR:
    STOSB                          ; Store the character in RESULT
    JMP NEXT_CHAR                  ; Repeat for next character

END_CONVERT:
    MOV AL, '$'                    ; Append string terminator
    STOSB

    MOV AH, 4CH                    ; Terminate the program
    INT 21H

CODE ENDS
END START

question: Explain different types of IO instructions. Differentiate between I/O mapped and memory mapped I/O.
answer:
The data movement between the CPU and peripheral devices is controlled by input/output (I/O) instructions. Typical I/O instruction types include:

  • IN Instruction: It is used to move data to the accumulator (AL or AX) from an input port. Example: IN AL, 03H
  • OUT Instruction: It is used to move data to an output port from the accumulator (AL or AX). Example: OUT 04H, AL
  • INS Instruction: It moves a string of data into memory from an input port. It use DI for memory and DX for port address.

Controlling communication with peripherals like as printers, keyboards, and other devices is made easier by these instructions.

question: What do you mean by vectored interrupt? Explain maskable and non-maskable interrupts in 8085 microprocessor.
answer:
A vectored interrupt is one in which the processor is aware of the interrupt’s address. Stated otherwise, the CPU is aware of the interrupt service routine’s address.To handle the interrupt, the CPU is guided to a particular memory region known as the interrupt vector. The address of the interrupt service routine (ISR) for the particular interrupt is contained at this place.

Maskable Interrupt No Maskable Interrupt
A maskable interrupt is a hardware interrupt that the CPU may direct to ignore or deactivate. A non-maskable interrupt that cannot be turned off or disregarded by CPU commands is known as a hardware interrupt.
After carrying out the current command, a maskable interrupt can be addressed. The current instructions and state are kept on the stack so that the CPU can handle non-maskable interrupts.
Lower priority jobs can be handled with the use of maskable interruptions. When handling higher priority jobs, such watchdog timers, non-maskable interrupts are helpful.
Maskable interruptions have a rapid reaction time. Response times for non-maskable interrupts are slow.
It may be vectored or non-vectored. All are vectored interrupts.

question: List out the limitation of parallel communication. Explain the different operation modes of 8255A PPI.
answer:
Limitations of Parallel Communication

  • Hardware requirement is complex.
  • It is only used for short distance communication.
  • It requires several cables, increasing the cost of implementation.
  • Maintaining signal timing over several lines is challenging.
  • Errors may result from interference between parallel lines.

fig : Internal Block Diagram of 8255A PPI

8255A is widely used programmable parallel I/O device. It can be programmed to transfer data under various conditions, from simple I/O to interrupt I/O. It is flexible, versatile and economical (when multiple I/O ports are required), but somewhat complex. It is an important general purpose I/O device that can be used with almost any microprocessor.

The 8255A is primarily operated in two modes: I/O (input/output) mode and the BSR(Bit Set Reset) mode. The BSR mode is used to set or reset the bit in port C. The I/O mode is further divided into three modes:

  • mode 0 : In this all ports function as simple I/O ports. It can set up port B and C.
  • mode 1 : It is a handshake mode. It can set up port B and C.
  • mode 2 : In this port A can be set up for bidirectional data transfer using handshake signal from port C.

question: What is Descriptor? Explain the use of segment descriptor in physical address conversion in 80826 microprocessor.
answer:
Descriptor is a data structure of CPU to specify the characteristics of a memory segment, including its size, base address, and access privileges.

A segment descriptor, which is kept in a descriptor table, is a component of the memory segmentation system of the 80826 microprocessor.This ensures efficient memory protection and management by defining limits and access rights for each memory segment. It is essential to the transformation of logical addresses into physical addresses. This is how it operates:

  • Segment Selector: The software offers a logical address that consists of an offset and a segment selector.
  • Access Descriptor Table: The segment descriptor in the descriptor table is referenced by the segment selector.
  • Information Extraction: The segment’s base address, limit, and access privileges are included in the segment description.
  • Determine Physical Address: To determine the physical address, the offset given in the logical address is multiplied by the base address from the descriptor.

question: What is ALE signal? Draw a timing diagram for LDA 5000H instruction and explain the machine cycles involved.
answer:
ALE (Address Latch Enable) is a control signal in the 8085 microprocessor used to demultiplex the address and data lines. Since the lower-order address (A0-A7) and data lines (D0-D7) share the same pins (AD0-AD7), the ALE signal indicates when these lines carry the address or data.

  • When ALE = High: The lines carry the address (A0-A7).
  • When ALE = Low: The lines carry data (D0-D7).

 

Opcode Fetch Cycle (T1-T4):

  • Purpose: Fetch the opcode (3AH) for the LDA instruction from the memory address pointed to by the Program Counter (PC).
  • Process:
    • T1: The low-order address (A0-A7) is placed on the multiplexed bus AD0-AD7, and ALE goes high to latch it.
    • T2-T4: The opcode (3AH) is fetched and stored in the instruction register. RD is active low during the read operation.

2. Memory Read Cycle 1 (T1-T3):

  • Purpose: Fetch the lower byte of the address (00H) for the memory location (5000H).
  • Process:
    • T1: The high-order address (A8-A15) is placed on the bus, and ALE is not active.
    • T2-T3: The lower byte (00H) is read from the memory.

3. Memory Read Cycle 2 (T1-T3):

  • Purpose: Fetch the high-order byte of the address (50H) for the memory location (5000H).
  • Process:
    • T1: The high-order address (A8-A15) is placed on the bus, and ALE remains inactive.
    • T2-T3: The higher byte (50H) is read from the memory.

4. Memory Read Cycle 3 (T1-T3):

  • Purpose: Fetch the data from memory location 5000H.
  • Process:
    • T1: The 16-bit address (5000H) is fully latched.
    • T2-T3: The data from memory location 5000H is read and placed in the accumulator.

question: Explain LHLD and SHLD instruction. Ten 8-bit data are stored at memory location starting from 6000H. Write an assembly program for 8085 microprocessor to calculate the sum of this data array and store the sum and carry starting from 9500H.
answer:
LHLD : It fills the H and L registers with information from two successive memory locations. The upper byte (from address + 1) goes to the H register, whereas the lower byte (from the provided address) goes to the L register.

eg: LHLD 5000H loads data from 5000H into L and 5001H into H.

SHLD : It stores information from the H and L registers in two memory regions that are sequential. The stated address contains the contents of the L register, while the next address (address + 1) contains the contents of the H register.

eg: Example: SHLD 5000H stores L in 5000H and H in 5001H.

LXI H, 6000H      ; Load starting address of data array into HL pair
LXI D, 0000H      ; Initialize DE pair to hold the sum (D: High byte, E: Low byte)
MVI C, 0AH        ; Load count (10 numbers) into register C

NEXT_BYTE:
MOV A, M          ; Move the data at memory address pointed by HL into A
ADD E             ; Add the content of A to the lower byte (E)
MOV E, A          ; Store the result back in E
MOV A, D          ; Move the higher byte of the sum into A
ADC A, 00H        ; Add the carry to the higher byte (D)
MOV D, A          ; Store the result back in D
INX H             ; Increment HL to point to the next data byte
DCR C             ; Decrement the count
JNZ NEXT_BYTE     ; If count is not zero, repeat the process

LXI H, 9500H      ; Load the destination address (9500H) to store the sum
MOV M, E          ; Store the lower byte of the sum at 9500H
INX H             ; Increment HL to point to the next memory location
MOV M, D          ; Store the higher byte (carry) of the sum at 9501H

HLT               ; Halt the program
